text: A Memphis household began receiving two utility bills. One named Willie S. Craft. The second account named Willie C. Craft: one middle initial apart.
provenance: Then, in 1973, the Crafts began receiving two bills: their regular bill, and a second bill with an account number in the name of Willie C. Craft, as opposed to Willie S. Craft.

text: The house had two gas and electric meter sets but only one water meter because the residence had previously been a duplex.
provenance: The residence had been used previously as a duplex.

text: That physical setup explains why two accounts could exist. It does not prove which charges were right or who caused the accounts to remain separate.
provenance: Nobody ever decided whether the Crafts owed the money.

text: The opinion's record points in conflicting directions about responsibility, so this Short does not blame the family, a contractor, or the utility.
provenance: Three courts, four years, and a record that never agreed with itself — all out of what happened at the other end of that line.

text: Mary Craft repeatedly tried to get an explanation after a final notice and told the office that she had paid a bill.
The Court's account says service was terminated five times for nonpayment. That count is attributed to the Court, not presented as an undisputed fact.
provenance: During this period, the Crafts' utility service was terminated five times for nonpayment.

text: And no court in this case decided whether the money on the disputed account was actually owed.
provenance: Not the trial court. Not the court of appeals. Not the Supreme Court.

text: The legal fight therefore grew from a record that could not settle its own starting point: Willie C. and Willie S., one letter apart.
